## Start with the first marimo notebook

Bring a laptop and charger. Try the [setup guide](../setup.qmd) beforehand if you can; an unfinished installation is fine. Download and extract the [introductory kit](../downloads/introductory-setup.zip). From its folder:

```bash
uv sync --locked
uv run --locked marimo edit notebooks/00-getting-started.py --headless
```

Open the local URL printed in the terminal. Change a concentration, follow the dependent cells, and check a prediction by hand. We will meet variables, lists, and a small function, and save our own notebook copy. The deliberately flawed error calculation is something to investigate as we go, not a prerequisite for following the lecture.

[First notebook](../notebooks/00-getting-started.py) · [Recorded preview](../notebooks/previews/00-getting-started.html)

## ML MolSim: a concise lecture

Our question is concrete: **can geometric descriptors predict simulated CO₂ uptake in a porous material?** We will follow one modelling workflow, keeping the kernel discussion visual:

1. **The MOF prediction task · 8 minutes.** Connect the eight supplied geometric descriptors to simulated CO₂ uptake at 298 K and 16 bar. Give the training, validation, and test rows distinct jobs.
2. **Fitting and regularisation · 15 minutes.** Connect a fitted line to several descriptors, compare with a median baseline, and explain overfitting and the regularisation setting `alpha`. Keep the error calculation to one short example.
3. **Nonlinear models and Gaussian kernels · 17 minutes.** Use the [three-point demonstration](../activities/kernel.html) to see how similarities and fitted coefficients produce a prediction. Explain the width setting `gamma` with a short worked example.
4. **Standardisation and pipelines · 11 minutes.** Ask what changing units does to a distance. Estimate scaling from training rows and reuse it when predicting validation or test rows.
5. **Model comparison and cross-validation · 12 minutes.** Compare the notebook's median baseline, scaled ridge, and unscaled/scaled kernel ridge models on the same validation rows. Introduce cross-validation as an extension of its fixed split, fitting preprocessing within each fold.
6. **Prediction plots, final assessment, and questions · 7 minutes.** Read parity and residual plots, record the model choice before revealing test results, and state which materials the test error might describe.

The [lecture slides for annotation](../downloads/11-november-ml-molsim.pdf) leave space for handwritten diagrams and worked examples. They follow the background and modelling workflow in the [original MolSim lecture](https://www.compchem.nl/wp-content/uploads/molsim2023/L09_Machine-Learning.pdf), with shorter error calculations.

The slides focus on the background needed to understand `03-mof-uptake.py`, with space to work through examples on the iPad. The geometric descriptors are already supplied, so their atomistic construction is outside this session. Use the 70-minute timetable as a guide and continue unfinished discussion in the supported practical. The [MOF notes](../lectures/03-mof-uptake.qmd) contain the fuller explanation. Detailed kernel derivations, feature importance, and bootstrap uncertainty remain for later lectures.

## Hands-on work: start when ready, continue on 2 December

Use the [MOF practical kit](../downloads/mof-practical.zip), extracted separately from the introductory kit. The [practical instructions](../lectures/03-mof-uptake.qmd#practical) explain how to open `03-mof-uptake.py`.

Start with the data, then the baseline, then the unscaled/scaled model comparison. Write down what you expect before running a comparison. Keep the test checkbox unchecked until you have recorded your model choice. Stop after the selected model's final assessment; the feature-importance and bootstrap sections are for later. Bring unfinished work and errors to the supported session on **2 December**; there is no expectation of completing the practical on 11 November.

The MOF notebook uses a fixed training/validation/test split. The [separate model-selection practical](../lectures/model-selection.qmd#why-cross-validation) provides a cross-validation exercise with a simulated dataset.
